questions.q: What is the fundamental physical property that allows distillation to separate a mixture of two miscible liquids?
questions.a: The fundamental property is the difference in boiling points of the two liquids. A wrong answer (e.g., "difference in density" or "difference in solubility") reveals the student is confusing distillation with separation by separating funnel (immiscible liquids) or crystallisation (solid-liquid solubility differences).

questions.q: Why is a fractionating column packed with glass beads or fitted with trays, and what would happen if you used a simple distillation setup for a mixture of acetone (b.p. 56°C) and methanol (b.p. 65°C)?
questions.a: The packing increases surface area for repeated condensation and vaporisation, enriching the vapour in the more volatile component each cycle. Without it, the vapours of both liquids would rise together and the distillate would be a mixture, not pure acetone. A wrong answer (e.g., "the beads prevent bumping") shows confusion with anti-bumping granules in the flask, not understanding the theoretical plate concept.

questions.q: A student sets up simple distillation to separate a mixture of ethanol (b.p. 78°C) and water (b.p. 100°C). The thermometer reads 82°C when the first drops collect. Explain whether this reading is expected and what it indicates about the distillate composition.
questions.a: The reading is higher than pure ethanol's boiling point because ethanol forms an azeotrope with water (95.6% ethanol, 4.4% water) boiling at 78.2°C; 82°C suggests the mixture is not yet at the azeotropic composition or the thermometer is not at the vapour exit. The distillate is ethanol-rich but not pure. A wrong answer (e.g., "thermometer is broken") misses the concept of azeotrope formation and non-ideal behaviour.

questions.q: Compare the energy changes in the distillation flask and the condenser during fractional distillation of crude oil. Why is the temperature gradient along the fractionating column essential?
questions.a: In the flask, heat energy overcomes intermolecular forces (endothermic vaporisation); in the condenser, heat is released (exothermic condensation). The temperature gradient (hot at bottom, cool at top) ensures each fraction condenses at its specific boiling point level. A wrong answer (e.g., "same temperature everywhere") ignores that separation relies on different condensation temperatures for different hydrocarbon chain lengths.

questions.q: A lab technician claims that simple distillation can completely separate a 50:50 mixture of benzene (b.p. 80°C) and toluene (b.p. 110°C) in one run. Evaluate this claim and justify your answer.
questions.a: The claim is partially correct because the 30°C difference allows good separation by simple distillation, but not 100% pure in one run; the first fractions will be benzene-rich, later fractions toluene-rich, and middle fractions mixed. For high purity, multiple redistillations or fractional distillation are needed. A wrong answer (e.g., "yes, because boiling points are different") overestimates simple distillation's efficiency for close-boiling mixtures.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using household items to demonstrate the principle of fractional distillation without a fractionating column, and explain how you would verify the separation.
questions.a: Use two pots: boil a mixture of water and vinegar (acetic acid b.p. 118°C) in one pot, place a smaller bowl floating inside to collect condensate, cover with an inverted lid filled with ice. The condensate will be mostly water (b.p. 100°C). Verify by smelling (vinegar smell remains in pot) or testing pH of condensate (neutral) vs residue (acidic). A poor answer (e.g., "just boil and collect") misses the need for temperature control and verification of separation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Distillation is a physical separation technique used to separate components of a homogeneous mixture of miscible liquids based on differences in their boiling points; simple distillation is effective when boiling points differ by more than 25°C, while fractional distillation uses a ______ column to achieve separation when boiling points are closer.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you have a bottle of homemade rose water that smells faintly of ______ because it was fermented slightly – you want pure rose water.
What is Distillation? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Distillation is a physical separation technique used to separate components of a homogeneous mixture of miscible liquids based on differences in their boiling points; simple distillation is effective when boiling points differ by more than 25°C, while fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to achieve separation when boiling.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Distillation is a physical separation technique used to separate components of a homogeneous mixture of miscible liquids based on differences in their boiling points; simple distillation is effective when boiling points differ by more than ______°C, while fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to achieve separation when boiling points are closer.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Distillation?
questions.a: Students often think the thermometer bulb should be dipped in the boiling liquid; actually it must be placed at the side-arm entrance so it reads the vapour temperature.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can explain the principle of distillation using particle theory, correctly choose between simple and fractional distillation for a given mixture, and draw labelled apparatus diagrams showing the direction of water flow in the condenser and the position of the thermometer bulb.
